one_liner: Multi-buffer SHA-256 that hashes 4 independent messages per AVX register with standard digests; 3.42x OpenSSL 1.0.1 on 4KB messages.
what_it_does: S-HASH is an algorithm, described in the paper as Algorithm 1, for hashing k independent messages of arbitrary lengths into k ordinary SHA-256 digests. It keeps 4 messages active, one per 32-bit lane of a 128-bit AVX register. When a lane's message runs out, it feeds that lane a padding block, then starts the next queued message. The interface is a batch call (arrays of buffers, lengths and output pointers), not per-message init/update/final. The authors released no code. The technique ships as Intel ISA-L crypto's sha256_mb (a submit/flush context manager), OpenSSL's internal sha256_multi_block, and minio/sha256-simd's AVX-512 server in Go.
how_it_is_fast: This is SIMD across messages ('multi-buffer', first tried by Aciicmez in 2004 on Pentium 4 SSE2 for a 1.71x gain). Each lane holds one message's state, so one S-UPDATE compresses four 64-byte blocks from four messages with the same instruction stream. The scheduler runs min(remaining length)/64 blocks at a time, then finalizes or refills the lanes that ran out, and finishes any leftover buffers serially. The paper gives two reasons it falls short of 4x on Sandy Bridge: the scalar ALU path is faster than the SIMD unit, and each SHA-256 rotate costs two SIMD shifts plus an xor instead of one ROR.
when_to_use: Many independent messages are ready at once and each needs a standard SHA-256 digest: boot-time integrity checks of OS components, dedup chunk fingerprints, file-tree manifests, or TLS/HMAC servers that batch work across connections (the paper's own scenarios).
Messages of similar length. Eight equal 17.76MB files reached 2.26x over OpenSSL from disk at native clock, against 1.73x for 350 mixed Windows driver files, because equal lanes finish together.
Data already in cache or RAM. On 4KB chunks, speed was flat at 5.18-5.21 c/B whether the data sat in L1, L2, LLC or main memory.
Wide-SIMD x86 without SHA extensions. AVX2 doubles the lane count to 8 and AVX-512 to 16. minio's README reports 3498 MB/s per core with 16-lane AVX-512 on a Xeon Platinum 8124M, 7.8x its AVX2 path.
when_not_to_use: One message at a time, or latency-bound single-stream hashing. Only one lane does useful work. For that, use a fast serial or SHA-extension SHA-256, or a tree mode such as j-lanes if you control the format.
Very uneven message sizes. Lanes stall until they are refilled and stragglers finish serially, which is why the mixed-size directory got only 1.73x.

Pipelines limited by I/O. At 3.3GHz, the 400MB/s SSD RAID0 equals about 7.15 c/B, so S-HASH reached 8.65 c/B from disk rather than 5.2. The abstract's '~6.73 c/B, almost 3x' needed the CPU down-clocked to 1.6GHz.

Small messages or thin batches. OpenSSL's multi-buffer notes say real-world gains on 2KB fragments are 75-130% on Haswell, against a 170% asymptotic figure. minio's README advises plain SHA-256 below about 1MB for its channel-scheduled server.

Code you would have to maintain yourself. Linux added AVX2 multibuffer SHA-256/512 in 4.8 (2016), then removed it in August 2018 because it was broken, too complex to maintain, and its 'performance benefits for real-world use cases are debatable'.

integration.form: not applicable: a paper only, with no S-HASH code released. The shipping equivalent is Intel ISA-L crypto sha256_mb, a C and assembly static or shared library.
integration.dependencies: not documented for the paper. ISA-L crypto needs nasm 2.14.01 or later on x86-64 per its README.
integration.min_toolchain: not documented: the paper gives no compiler or flags. ISA-L crypto builds with gcc, clang, icc or MSVC 2019+, and on aarch64 with gas 2.34+ and gcc 8+.
integration.platforms: The paper measured x86-64 with AVX (Core i5-2500, Sandy Bridge, Fedora 16). ISA-L crypto's sha256_mb has SSE, AVX, AVX2 and AVX-512 (4, 8 and 16 lanes) plus SHA-NI variants, and aarch64 code, with runtime dispatch.
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the paper. In ISA-L the context manager is a mutable scheduler object, and its header does not state a threading contract.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the digests are byte-identical to SHA256(), but the caller must batch many messages through a submit/flush (or array) interface instead of the per-message init/update/final or one-shot API.

gotchas: Completion is decoupled from submission. ISA-L processes jobs out of order and returns a context only when its lane finishes, so callers must keep submitting or call flush to drain. The paper itself says the software needs restructuring to benefit.
The 2.25x figure is against the authors' own n-SMS serial code, which is also their OpenSSL RT #2784 patch, not against a third-party implementation. The 3.42x figure is against stock OpenSSL 1.0.1.
The disk results are in cycles/byte, so down-clocking flatters them. At 1.6GHz, S-HASH on the UNIFORM files is 6.73 c/B but only 226.73 MB/s, against 363.83 MB/s at 3.3GHz.
OpenSSL's sha256_multi_block is internal. It is used only by the AES-CBC-HMAC-SHA256 multi-block TLS cipher code and cannot be reached as a general multi-message digest API.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose S-HASH (in practice ISA-L's sha256_mb) over j-lanes when you have many independent messages and need interoperable standard SHA-256 digests. j-lanes speeds up a single message but changes the digest. In Go, minio/sha256-simd already ships the same multi-buffer idea as its AVX-512 server alongside a drop-in crypto/sha256 replacement, so use it rather than porting the paper.
verified_claims_summary: On a Core i5-2500 (Sandy Bridge, 3.3GHz; Turbo, HT and SpeedStep off; Fedora 16), 4-buffer AVX SHA-256 hashed 4KB chunks at 5.18-5.21 c/B from L1 through main memory. Serial OpenSSL 1.0.1 took 17.72-17.80 c/B (3.42x) and the authors' n-SMS took 11.68-11.81 c/B (2.25x). Hashing files from a two-SSD RAID0 at native clock gave 8.65 vs 19.55 c/B (2.26x) for eight equal 17.76MB files and 17.53 vs 30.32 c/B (1.73x) for 350 mixed-size files. No compiler or flags are stated.
status_note: This is finished 2012 research (ePrint 2012/371, republished in Journal of Information Security 3(4):319-325, a SCIRP journal, 9 Crossref citations) with no code of its own. The technique is maintained in Intel ISA-L crypto (last push 2026-07) and survives inside OpenSSL's TLS multi-block path, while Linux dropped its copy in 2018.
